title: A booster pump's power curve, exact in both directions

blocks.text: A water utility models the electricity drawn by a booster pump station as a function of the flow it delivers. The pump's measured curve is given as breakpoints `xs` (flow, L/s, starting at 0) and `ys` (power, kW), with straight lines in between:

The pump is most efficient in the middle band, so the slopes fall and then rise: the curve is neither convex nor concave. The station's model uses the power in two places, as a cost in the energy bill and as a load that a backup generator must be able to carry, so the power is pushed down in one row and up in another. The pump cannot deliver more than the last breakpoint's flow.

The model in `booster.py` has two continuous variables, `flow >= 0` and `power` (free). Write `add_power_curve(model, flow, power, xs, ys)` so that the model allows exactly the pairs `(flow, power)` that lie on the curve. Add whatever variables you need. The tests use other curves too.
With $`(X_j, F_j)`$, $`j = 0, \dots, K`$, the breakpoints, the model so far is
Neither push nor shape helps here, so every point must be tied to one segment. The lesson's lambda form is one way; any formulation that allows exactly the curve's points passes.
The tests fix the flow and the power and ask the solver whether the model accepts the pair, so any correct formulation passes. About ten lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt


def add_power_curve(model: mathopt.Model, flow: mathopt.Variable, power: mathopt.Variable,
                    xs: tuple[float, ...], ys: tuple[float, ...]) -> None:
    """Rows that make power = f(flow) exactly, for the curve through (xs[j], ys[j])."""
    pick, part_flow, part_power = [], [], []
    for s in range(len(xs) - 1):
        on = model.add_binary_variable(name=f"on_{s}")                  # the pump runs in band s
        q = model.add_variable(lb=0, name=f"q_{s}")                    # the flow, if in band s, else 0
        model.add_linear_constraint(q >= xs[s] * on, name=f"band_lo_{s}")
        model.add_linear_constraint(q <= xs[s + 1] * on, name=f"band_hi_{s}")
        rate = (ys[s + 1] - ys[s]) / (xs[s + 1] - xs[s])
        pick.append(on)
        part_flow.append(q)
        part_power.append((ys[s] - rate * xs[s]) * on + rate * q)
    model.add_linear_constraint(sum(pick) == 1, name="one_band")
    model.add_linear_constraint(flow == sum(part_flow), name="flow_parts")
    model.add_linear_constraint(power == sum(part_power), name="power_parts")


def build(xs: tuple[float, ...], ys: tuple[float, ...]) -> tuple[mathopt.Model, mathopt.Variable, mathopt.Variable]:
    model = mathopt.Model(name="booster")
    flow = model.add_variable(lb=0, name="flow")
    power = model.add_variable(lb=-1e9, ub=1e9, name="power")
    add_power_curve(model, flow, power, xs, ys)
    return model, flow, power


if __name__ == "__main__":
    model, flow, power = build((0, 20, 40, 60, 80), (0, 30, 42, 70, 120))
    print(model.get_num_linear_constraints(), "rows")

# A fan's curve: flow and power, slopes 2.0, 0.5, 1.5.
xs, ys = (0, 10, 30, 50), (0, 20, 30, 60)

def accepted(model):
    params = mathopt.SolveParameters(time_limit=timedelta(seconds=5))
    result = mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.HIGHS, params=params)
    return result.termination.reason == mathopt.TerminationReason.OPTIMAL


def allowed(flow, power):
    model, q, p = build(xs, ys)
    q.lower_bound = q.upper_bound = flow
    p.lower_bound = p.upper_bound = power
    return accepted(model)

a power a little below or above the curve at a mid-segment flow is refused

origin.section: One Binary per Segment Enforces the Neighbour Rule

concepts: only two neighbouring weights may be positive, the SOS2 rule
one binary per segment writes the neighbour rule for a curve of any shape
a point of the curve as weights on the breakpoints, and why weights alone are not enough
